content: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a condition linked to numerous adverse health outcomes for both mothers and their infants, with effects that can persist in the short and long term. The global prevalence of GDM is rising, necessitating the evaluation of preventive strategies, such as combined dietary and exercise interventions. This review aimed to assess the impact of these interventions on preventing GDM and its associated complications. The review included 23 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 8,918 pregnant women and 8,709 infants. These studies compared combined diet and exercise interventions to standard care (no intervention). The interventions and outcomes varied across studies, and none of the trials reported funding from pharmaceutical companies or organizations with vested interests. The overall risk of bias was unclear due to insufficient methodological details in the studies. Most of the trials were conducted in high-income countries. The findings suggested a potential reduction in the risk of GDM in the group receiving combined diet and exercise interventions compared to the standard care group. The average risk ratio (RR) was 0.85, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.71 to 1.01, based on moderate-quality evidence. There was also a possible reduction in the risk of cesarean section (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.02, moderate-quality evidence). However, no significant differences were observed between the groups for pre-eclampsia (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.22, low-quality evidence), pregnancy-induced hypertension or hypertension (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.27, very low-quality evidence), perinatal mortality (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.63, low-quality evidence), or large-for-gestational-age infants (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.07, low-quality evidence). Data on infant mortality or morbidity were not reported. Subgroup analyses based on trial design, maternal body mass index (BMI), and ethnicity did not reveal any clear differences in treatment effects. The impact of maternal age, parity, and specific features of the diet and exercise interventions could not be assessed due to insufficient data. Sensitivity analyses, which considered the quality of the RCTs, generally supported the main findings. For secondary outcomes, no significant differences were observed between the intervention and control groups for perineal trauma (RR 1.27, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.05, moderate-quality evidence), neonatal hypoglycemia (RR 1.42, 95% CI 0.67 to 2.98, low-quality evidence), or childhood adiposity (BMI z-score: mean difference [MD] 0.05, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.40, low-quality evidence). However, the intervention group experienced less gestational weight gain compared to the control group (MD -0.89 kg, 95% CI -1.39 to -0.40, moderate-quality evidence). Data on maternal postnatal depression, type 2 diabetes, childhood/adulthood type 2 diabetes, or neurosensory disability were not reported. The authors concluded that moderate-quality evidence supports the potential benefits of combined diet and exercise interventions during pregnancy in reducing the risks of GDM, cesarean section, and excessive gestational weight gain. However, no clear differences were observed for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, perinatal mortality, large-for-gestational-age infants, perineal trauma, neonatal hypoglycemia, or childhood adiposity. The quality of evidence ranged from moderate to very low, with limitations due to study design issues, imprecision, and, in some cases, unexplained inconsistencies. The variability in the diet and exercise components across studies limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions for clinical practice. Future research should provide more detailed descriptions of the interventions, assess their impact on behavior change, and aim for standardization across studies. Additionally, the use of core outcome sets could improve the consistency of reporting.
